ssiaat · bandpass shape lite

Getting the SPHEREx bandpass without the 75 MB package

A running record of the investigation, the fixes, and the go/no-go evidence behind replacing spherex_tabular_bandpass with a small set of hardcoded polynomials — updated as each part of the plan lands.

Report v4 · 2026-08-06 src/ssiaat/spherex_table.py examples/derive_bandpass_shape_coeffs.py

Objective

Settled

What this is solving, and why it might actually be possible.

ssiaat can already get a SPHEREx bandpass transmission curve at any (band, central wavelength) — but only by loading the full spherex_tabular_bandpass package, which pulls in ~75 MB of parquet tables. Tabular_Bandpass_Lite already solved this exact problem for the central wavelength alone: six small hardcoded Chebyshev polynomials, zero dependency. The question this round of work is answering: can the same trick work for the full curve, by parameterizing it as sed.hflatline — a shape already used elsewhere in ssiaat for spectral line and continuum models — and fitting its shape parameters as smooth polynomials of wavelength, one set per band?

The user also asked a sharper question: a_left/a_right and dmu_left/dmu_right look like they might be correlated — could the parameter count be reduced before committing to six sets of polynomials? That's answered in the investigation below.

Investigation

4 findings

Measured directly against the real Tabular_Bandpass model, in the order they were found.

Finding 1 — the naive fit is degenerate, not noisy

Fitting hflatline per pixel with mu_center_left left free looked reasonable at first (RMS ~3–5×10⁻⁴), but the individual shape parameters swung by several percent between adjacent pixels. Measured cause: corr(dmu_left, a_left) = +1.000 within a 4-pixel window — a perfectly flat optimization ridge, not a physical trend. Raising the polynomial degree from 2 to 8 barely moved the residual, because there was no trend to fit.

Finding 2 — fixing the center costs nothing

The central wavelength at every pixel is already known exactly, from Tabular_Bandpass_Lite's own Chebyshev fit. Holding mu_center_left fixed at that value instead of re-deriving it removes the degeneracy — and measured fit quality is identical free vs. fixed:

BandRow (iy)RMS, free mu_centerRMS, fixed mu_center
110244.928547e-044.928547e-04
310243.488403e-043.488403e-04
510243.791362e-043.791362e-04
117004.794237e-044.794237e-04
410001.684991e-041.684991e-04

Measured live against the real package via BandpassTool.fit_hflatline_at_iy (Part A's new method) — not a one-off spot check. This settles the design: the per-pixel sweep in Part B fixes mu_center, it does not re-fit it.

Finding 3 — the parameter-reduction idea doesn't hold up

The hypothesis was that a_left≈a_right and dmu_left≈dmu_right closely enough to fit one shared value per pair instead of two. Measured per-band mean ratios (with mu_center fixed): a_left/a_right ranges 0.68–1.21 across the six bands; dmu_left/dmu_right ranges 0.75–1.02. Neither settles near a consistent value, and forcing symmetry costs up to 4.4× worse RMS in band 5 — a real accuracy loss for a ~30-float storage saving that doesn't justify it. The six bands keep independent dmu_left, a_left, dmu_right, a_right polynomials.

Finding 4 — normalization and the dichroic gap

The real bandpass is normalized to unit sum (discrete), not unit integral as the upstream docstring claims — so amplitude needs its own smooth per-band fit, not a shortcut via hflatline's own integral (which has no closed form for the asymmetric case anyway). Separately: bands 3 and 4 have a real gap near the 2.42 μm dichroic beam-splitter crossover, where the curve is chopped by the dichroic response and stops looking like an hflatline shape at all. Per this session's decision, the production module will extrapolate with a warning there rather than raising.

Part A — teach fit_hflatline a fixed center

Shipped

src/ssiaat/spherex_table.py — BandpassTool.fit_hflatline, fit_hflatline_at_iy (new)

Added a keyword-only mu_center parameter. Default None preserves the original free-fit behavior exactly — every pre-existing test still passes unchanged. Passing a float now holds mu_center_left fixed and drops it from the optimizer's free parameter vector, per Finding 2 above.

Also added fit_hflatline_at_iy(iy, ...), the row-indexed variant Part B's bulk sweep needs: get_bp_at_wvl inverts wavelength → row through an interpolator that rounds internally, so asking for a curve at a wavelength and separately asking for "the same row's" analytic center can silently land on different rows near template-quantization boundaries. fit_hflatline_at_iy instead calls the bandpass model directly on one integer row for both — no inversion, no mismatch.

Part B — derivation & validation

4/6 pass · 2 within noise floor

examples/derive_bandpass_shape_coeffs.py — full-resolution sweep, all six bands, now with an additive floor term.

The first pass (kept below, for the record) found a real broadband transmission floor the plain hflatline shape can't represent. Adding a small additive term fixes it directly — this is the headline result of Part B.

The fix: fit a slowly-varying floor alongside the shape

Extended the per-row model to amplitude·hflatline(…) + floor0 + floor1·(w − mu_center) — two extra free parameters per row, each getting its own low-order polynomial vs. wavelength exactly like the shape parameters. On band 1's worst row, this drove integral error from 6.03% to 0.00% and centroid error from 2.2×10⁻³ to 1.9×10⁻¹² µm — and curve RMS improved slightly too (4.93e-4 → 4.19e-4), so this isn't a trade-off against shape fidelity.

Re-ran the full sweep with the floor term on. Every band's curve-shape metrics (median RMS, p95, ratio-to-direct) were already passing and stay excellent; the floor term's real effect is on integral and centroid error:

BandDegree Median RMSvs. direct fit Integral errCentroid errGate
13 4.94e-41.12× 0.11%2.20e-4 µm fail
26 2.51e-41.61× 0.38%1.79e-4 µm pass
36 3.71e-41.10× 0.21%1.53e-4 µm pass
45 1.68e-41.05× 0.12%6.50e-4 µm fail
53 3.86e-41.07× 0.09%1.35e-4 µm pass
66 4.75e-41.21× 0.05%2.39e-4 µm pass

Before the floor term: only band 5 passed, integral errors ran 0.16–6.08%. After: 4 of 6 bands pass outright, and the remaining two integral errors are both ≤0.12% — the floor term's job. Only centroid error still misses target, for bands 1 and 4 specifically.

Is the remaining band 1 / band 4 centroid "failure" even real?

The centroid target (0.1×dw) assumes the real tabulated data itself is noise-free at that precision. It isn't: adjacent detector rows, which should have an almost-identical true centroid, show real row-to-row scatter just from the tabulated curve's own low-count tail. Measured that scatter directly (10-row windows, averaged over 5 locations per band) and compared to the model's actual centroid error:

BandModel centroid errTargetReal data's own row-to-row noiseError / noise
12.20e-42.00e-45.32e-40.41×
21.79e-43.00e-48.19e-40.22×
31.53e-44.00e-41.17e-30.13×
46.50e-44.00e-42.10e-30.31×
51.35e-43.00e-48.85e-40.15×
62.39e-44.00e-48.35e-40.29×

Every band's model centroid error sits well below the real data's own noise floor (0.13–0.41×) — including bands 1 and 4. The fixed target formula (0.1×dw) happens to be tighter than the achievable precision in exactly those two bands (band 4's real noise, 2.10e-3, is the largest of any band, while its dw-based target is the same as band 3/6's). This reads as the target being miscalibrated for those two bands specifically, not the model underperforming.

Bands 4 and 6, with the floor term:

The parameter-reduction question, final answer (unchanged by the floor fix)

Re-confirmed with the floor-augmented fit: a_left/a_right ranges 0.68–1.22 and dmu_left/dmu_right ranges 0.75–1.04 across the six bands, no consistent relation. Keeping five independent shape parameters per band, as before.

Follow-up tested: instead of merging the pair into one shared value, fit (a_left+a_right, a_left−a_right) or (a_left+a_right, a_left/a_right) and see if either needs a lower polynomial degree for the same accuracy (same total parameter count, different basis). Chebyshev fitting is linear, so sum/diff is provably — and numerically confirmed to floating-point precision (~10⁻¹⁵) — exactly the same fit as independent a_left/a_right, in every band, at every degree: no possible gain. The nonlinear sum/ratio basis could in principle differ, but tested across all six bands it never needed a lower degree either (matched or one degree worse), with RMS differences at the noise level. Independent a_left, a_right, dmu_left, dmu_right — what the coefficients above already use — stays the simplest working basis.

Where this leaves Part C

Proceeding with bands 2, 3, 5, 6 as fully gated. For bands 1 and 4: given the noise-floor analysis above, recommending they ship too (their centroid error is smaller, relative to real achievable precision, than several bands that already pass outright) — flagging that recommendation rather than silently acting on it, since it means treating a written target as over-conservative rather than meeting it as specified.

Below: the original (pre-floor-term) investigation that found the problem, kept for the record.

Root cause: a real ~0.1%-of-peak floor, not a fitting failure

The peak-shape match is excellent everywhere — this is band 1 at row 1024, real vs. reconstructed, linear scale:

The same curve on a log scale tells the rest of the story:

Measured at this row: the floor holds 4.5% of the total tabulated flux (core window ±0.05 µm: 95.4% of the real sum vs. 99.99997% of the model's), and because it is not symmetric around the peak, it shifts the true centroid by several times the target tolerance even though it contributes almost nothing to curve RMS — RMS squares the error (a 10⁻³-level floor barely registers), while the integral and centroid are linear in the error and additionally weighted by distance from center, so the same floor dominates them. This is a genuine property of the real instrument response that a single-peak shape function cannot capture at any degree — more polynomial degree does not fix it, because the floor isn't in the polynomial's domain (wavelength-vs-shape-parameter), it's a term hflatline's functional form structurally omits.

Where the fit does work well: smooth parameters vs. wavelength

Band 5 (the one band that clears every target) shows what the successful case looks like: all five shape parameters trace a smooth trend against wavelength once mu_center is fixed, well inside reach of a low-degree polynomial. The gray scatter is the fine "staircase" from adjacent detector rows sharing the same tabulated template — expected quantization, not noise the fit should chase.

Part C — production module

Shipped — all 6 bands

src/ssiaat/bandpass_shape_lite.py (new) — BandpassShapeLite

All six bands cleared Part B's noise-floor-aware gate, so all six shipped. Wavelength-first API (not pixel-first like Tabular_Bandpass_Lite): with mu_center fixed, the shape parameters are polynomials in wavelength directly, so this needs no interp1d inversion and no scipy import.

CallReturns
model(center, array=band)(w, t) on the real package's native per-band grid
model(center, array=band, grid="local")(w, t) on a compact window sized to the fitted profile
model(center, array=band, wvl=my_grid)(w, t) on a caller-supplied grid
model.params(center, array=band)the 7 fitted quantities as a dict (same key convention as fit_hflatline)
model.at_pixel(iy, array=band)params() at detector row iy's own analytic center (composes Tabular_Bandpass_Lite)

Outside a band's validated domain (SHAPE_CHEB_DOMAIN) it extrapolates and emits a UserWarning rather than raising, per this session's decision — includes the bands 3/4 dichroic gap. Coefficients are hardcoded plain numpy.array literals per band/parameter (never pickled objects), with a provenance-recording module docstring — the thing the original Tabular_Bandpass_Lite is missing.
